utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody, and welcome back after the short recess. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Lazarevic, and then the absence of Mr. Sarapa, unless he is hidden behind the column. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye. Yes. The witness is already in the courtroom, so I will address him straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On behalf of the Trial Chamber, my colleagues, and also on behalf of the Tribunal I want to welcome you. You're about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, you're required to make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. The text is going to be handed to you. It's equivalent to a note. It's an undertaking. Please read it out aloud and that will be your undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. You're going to be asked questions first by Mr. Vanderpuye, I understand, who I'm sure you have already met, and he will then be followed by the various Defence teams on cross-examination. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ristic. I'm just going to ask you first to state your name for the record, spell your last name if you could.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Lazar Ristic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before I start examining you, I'm just going to point out a couple of things. One is to try and keep your voice up so that the interpreters can hear you, and also to allow a short pause between the question and answer so that there is time for the translations to occur so that we can all understand and follow what you say. First I want to ask you, have you had an opportunity to review certain statements that you've made concerning the events of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to those statements, did you review a statement that's dated 8th April 2004?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you review a statement that's dated 23rd of August, 2003?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you review a transcript of an interview that was conducted with the Office of the Prosecutor in October of 2005?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And aside from certain facts that you may wish to explain or further elaborate upon in your testimony, are you satisfied that with regard to what you actually said that those statements are -- are accurate?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Everything is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, I'm just going to ask you a few questions by way of background preliminarily. Can you tell us what your current employment is and how long you've been engaged in that occupation?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I work on maintaining electrical equipment in a factory in Birac. I've been working there for 28 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us when it was -- well, first of all, can you tell us when it was that you were first mobilised to the army of Republika Srpska, the VRS?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: First we organised ourselves on our own with the assistance of the Crisis Staff from Zvornik. We organised village guards in various villages starting in April -- and then starting in April 1992, I got involved in the war activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us when it was that you were demobilised?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: June of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And at the time that you were demobilised, can you tell us what your rank was?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: At the time when I was demobilised I was second lieutenant, and I was promoted to that rank in January of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to go briefly through the various positions that you had while you were active in the VRS, and I wondered if you can tell us what responsibilities and positions you held during your tenure.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: From the 1st of June, 1992, I started as a platoon commander in my town, and then in 1993, in March, I transferred to the battalion command as assistant commander for security. I remained in that post for two years, following which I became assistant commander of the battalion for the 4th Infantry Battalion within the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In your capacity as the assistant commander for security, did you have the opportunity to work with Milorad Trbic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us in what -- in what way that occurred? What was your relationship professionally with Mr. Trbic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Security organ of the battalion had certain tasks in relation to the security service of the brigade. We followed enemy forces which were facing the front part of our defence. In addition to that, we also dealt with the discipline within the unit, took into custody soldiers who deserted or created trouble. So Trbic would occasionally come to the brigade, or he would substitute for the commander, but we didn't come across each other frequently. It was rather rare that we cooperated. We cooperated more with the security chief. We mostly cooperated with him, and if he was absent then with his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And with respect to Mr. Trbic, can you tell us what his position was at the time, at this time that we're talking about now?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: At the time when he was in the brigade he was deputy or assistant chief for security in the Zvornik Brigade. Either deputy or assistant, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you have an opportunity to work with or have contact with Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And this is still in your capacity as an assistant commander for security in the 4th Battalion. Could you tell us what capacity -- in what capacity you had contact with Mr. Nikolic and what your professional relationship was?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Whenever there was a problem related to that type of work we asked for assistance in the brigade. We turned to the chief of security himself. There were meetings scheduled by him where we discussed problems in various battalions, which is to say that security officers from all battalions would attend those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the position that was occupied by Mr. Nikolic at that time was what, just so we're clear for the record.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Chief of security of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you -- did you have a -- a personal relationship, I would say, with either Mr. Trbic or Mr. Nikolic during that period of time while you were the assistant commander for security?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: It was nothing special, not a special relationship or anything of that sort. We cooperated fairly, and there was no particular relationship. It's just that I worked more with Mr. Nikolic than with Mr. Trbic. I knew Trbic very little because for a long time he was deputy commander in an another battalion and I don't know when exactly he came to the brigade, but he stayed there only shortly while I was with the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, I guess what I mean by the question is whether or not you had any opportunity to see them socially, that is, outside of a professional capacity.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: We had no time for socialising. I had a very good relationship with all officers within the brigade, so I treated them all equally.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I think you indicated that at some point you were appointed deputy commander of the 4th Infantry Battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And -- and when was that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date, but I think it was in March or early April of 1995. At around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, was that the position that you held in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Until the 1st of July, 1995. And then on the 1st of July, battalion commander went for training in Banja Luka, where he remained until the 18th of July, at which time he returned in the afternoon on the 18th of July. While he was absent, I acted as battalion commander and deputy commander simultaneously, which is to say that nobody was appointed to his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, just so that you can orient us to the scope of your command, the purview of your command, could you tell us how the 4th Infantry Battalion is organised, how it was organised in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Our area of responsibility of the front end went from Parlog to Pandurica. The battalion command or headquarters was stationed in Rebici, in Baljkovica near the front end of the defence lines. This is also the place where our logistics company was stationed as well as Intervention Platoon, which is to say that everything was in Baljkovica. The task of the battalion was to hold the lines of the front end of defence and to maintain control together with neighbouring battalions, and to cooperate with the brigade which was in Karakaj. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay, and can you tell us approximately how many men comprised this battalion?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I don't have the exact figures, but I think that there were about 450 or maybe more soldiers in the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did the battalion consist of several infantry companies within it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes. It had three infantry companies at the defence line. It had an anti-armoured platoon which was known under that name but was similar to an infantry unit. It had 25 people in it. In addition to this, we also had a logistics company, a mortar platoon, an intervention platoon, and the battalion command or headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And as a deputy commander of this battalion, can you tell us what you were specifically in charge of?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: While the battalion commander was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: While the battalion commander was there, yes.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Deputy commander of the battalion, when the commander is present, had certain tasks when touring the lines, which was performed on a daily basis. Deputy commander also substituted for the commander when the commander was absent, when the commander was on leave or attended some meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When the commander was absent was it the responsibility of the deputy commander to assume all of his responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what the responsibilities, therefore, as a commander of a battalion are or would have been at that time?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Everything that concerns the area of responsibility, the work of the battalion, was something that the battalion commander was responsible for in a way. The entire organisation went through the battalion commander, who was assisted by other members of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, as an acting deputy commander, can you tell us who you were reportable to? Who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't think he ever said acting deputy commander, just for the sake of clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: He's correct, I misspoke. I'll withdraw it and rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon, and you too, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As an acting commander -- all right. Let me rephrase the question again. As a deputy commander when you are assuming the responsibilities of the commander, can you tell us who you were reported -- reportable to? Who do you report to in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: To the brigade command. When the battalion commander is absent, the deputy commander takes over his responsibilities, is responsible and receives orders from the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And during the period that you were responsible for the command of the battalion between the 1st of July, 1995, and the 18th of July, 1995, did you report to the brigade command and receive orders from the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And to whom in particular were you responsible?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: To the brigade commander, who also stood in for the brigade commander who was absent in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And who was that person?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Major Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is he the individual that stood in for the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the brigade commander was whom? The absent brigade commander was whom?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in July when you were standing in for the commander of the battalion, did you receive certain information regarding an operation in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us what information you received and from whom you received it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: There was a meeting held at the brigade headquarters. I think it was on the 1st of July. The brigade commander explained at the meeting the work that was to take place in the coming period. He said that he was going to Srebrenica with a certain number of troops and that we were to remain and that Major Obrenovic would be in charge and that we needed to take care of battalions and everything else related to that in normal activities as it was until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in relation to that endeavour, did you assign any men to participate in that operation?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I did not assign anyone. It's the commander who said that my intervention platoon would be going with them to that area, to Srebrenica, and that they needed to be ready on the 4th of July, and their assembly point would be Konjevic Polje. So they should be ready on the 4th of July, and ready at the assembly point in Konjevic Polje to be ready to go to Srebrenica. And that's what I did. I sent them first home for a couple of days to get ready, and then they went off on that assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you apprised of what the purpose of that intervention unit was to be, what they were going to be used for specifically?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I didn't know how that would be done. All I knew was that they were going with him, and I needed no further explanation because they were going to accompany the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, can I be clear. The brigade commander who presided the meeting of 1st of July, was it Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think I'll put that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think you've heard the Judge's question. Perhaps you could -- okay. I think you've answered it, but I don't see a translation on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, you have to repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that 1st July meeting at the brigade it was Mr. Pandurevic who chaired, the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you receive any further information at a later point with respect to the men that had been assigned -- well, not assigned, I should say that went with the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: We received information through a cable by our signalsman, through radio signals, that on the 6th of July the attack on Srebrenica had begun. We also received a telegram saying that Srebrenica was taken on the 17th of July, and that's all the information we received at the battalion from the area of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I see in the record here that you received a telegram saying that Srebrenica was taken on the 17th of July. Is that your recollection or is that a mistranslation?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I think it was a misinterpretation; I said the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If I could just refer you to the 12th of July, 1995. Now, on that day did you have the opportunity to assign an intervention squad to the area of Tisova Kova [sic]?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of July I received a telegram from the brigade instructing me to form a platoon out of companies that were deployed on the front end of the defence line and send them in the evening to Tisova Kosa, and that's what I did. I communicated to company commanders to send me six, seven soldiers each depending on how many they could afford and that these men should report to the brigade command. I explained it was an order from the brigade command geared at preventing a rear attack on our defence line because the assumption was that certain forces from Srebrenica could get through and jeopardise our line of defence. When these people arrived, around 20 of them, there were ordinary people from companies. For the sake of security I sent our man from the command, one signalsman, to be with them. That man was slightly more capable than the rest of them, and he was named leader to keep a line of communication during that assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you just tell us approximately how many men you sent into that area?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Around 20, plus that man from the battalion command and the signalsman. And the signalsman had a RUP 12 device.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it was your understanding at the time you sent these men into that area that they were sent there because the area was in fact vulnerable?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you receive any information from the brigade command later on that evening, that is, the evening of the 12th of July, regarding the movement of the Muslims coming out of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Sometime after 2100 hours the operations officer on duty called us to tell us the large number of members of the Muslim army from Srebrenica, along with civilians, had set out towards Crni Vrh. They could not intercept them, and they could not divert them. I mean, members of the brigade led by Major Obrenovic. We received a dispatch from the brigade that they would be moving through -- through fields towards Nezuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And what was the position of the brigade in response to this advance by the Muslim members of the army and civilians from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Nobody told us much about that except for that telegram that arrived from the brigade telling us about the route of their movement. Nobody gave us any other information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have a planned response to that information within your battalion?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Since in that period we did not have a brigade commander and the chief of staff was busy with that interception, we up at the battalion did not have occasion to discuss these events. Instead, we had to organise our defence ourselves, as well as the work of the battalion as best we saw fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in the translation here I see that you have a reference to the chief of staff and also that he was busy with an interception. I just wondered if we could just clarify that so that it's clear on the record. When you say the chief of staff, whom are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Major Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when you say that he was busy with that interception, can you just describe what it is you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I think I called the duty operations officer, because in the presence of the commander and the chief of staff the battalions first talked to the duty operations officer, and if we needed to speak to the chief of staff or the commander of the brigade, we first requested all information from the duty operations officer, and therefore on that occasion since I assumed that could be dangerous for my battalion as well, I asked to speak to the chief of staff and I was told that he was in the area of Snagovo and that he was not available. So after that I didn't even ask to communicate with him any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And, sir, when you say "interception" do you mean that that was some kind of military operation with respect to confronting the -- the Muslims coming out of Srebrenica, the column?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I don't know how he was going about it, but I know that he was not successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me draw your attention to the 13th of July if I could. Now, you've indicated previously that the 4th Battalion had a mortar platoon. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: A mortar platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, a platoon.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And did you receive any information with regard to that platoon from the brigade command on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, I was informed from the brigade that a platoon was coming to my aid, a platoon from the 3rd infantry battalion to the Motovo intersection and Grujici location. They were supposed to help out with the security support provided to the mortar platoon. When the commander of the mortar platoon notified me they had arrived, I told them to come to see me personally. I gave them code-names for communications. And together with the commander of the mortar platoon I deployed them at the location above Krizevacke Nijve, divided into three groups, and they had received their assignment, namely to prepare for defence by means of making fortifications and shelters in case there should be combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us approximately how many men were assigned -- well, were sent to that area?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I didn't count them, but I think there were no more than 25. Twenty to 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were they sent to you because the battalion was unable or incapable at that time of protecting the mortar platoon through its own devices, its own men?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: It's not I who requested them. It was an assessment of the people from the brigade that I could use them. Maybe I could have a protected my mortar platoon with my own platoon, the one that had been busy making ambushes at Tisova Kosa. But instead I was just informed that men had arrived to assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when those men arrived, I think you indicated they were from the 3rd Infantry Battalion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when they arrived did they then fall under your command as the persons standing in for the commander of the 4th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as they came to see me, when I gave them code-names so that they should be part of our radio network system, they were under my direct command from that point on. And on that day I deployed them. And if they had stayed, they would be within my jurisdiction and under my command because they were within my zone of responsibility, manning mortars that belonged to my platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, let me draw your attention to the 14th of July, if I could. Do you remember the events of that day?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And on that day did you have the occasion to send an intervention battalion to the Snagovo area?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: That morning, following orders from Major Obrenovic, I sent a platoon from the 3rd Infantry Battalion to the area of Snagovo to report to Major Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recall how you received that order from Major Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I can't remember after all this time through what kind of communications and how, but I know for sure that the order came from Major Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is it possible that you could have had a conversation with the major the morning of the 14th?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I can't recall that kind of detail, because we had dedicated signalsmen who were on duty at the battalion, and we just received telegrams from them, or calls, and I can't remember whether it was through the RUP 12 device or otherwise, because it's the signalsmen who were in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can I ask you generally did you have occasion to speak to or communicate, I should say, with Major Obrenovic at any other time on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I did not. Not that I remember. In fact, I don't think that we had any contact at all until the afternoon of the 15th when he came to the battalion command personally. If there had been any talks, that could have been only in the form of orders being passed through signalsmen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to your recollection of this order to assign these men to the Snagovo area, was there anything else, according to your recollection, that was discussed or information that was exchanged?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: With Major Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, with Major Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember we talked that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you aware whether or not Major Obrenovic had any communication or his signalsman had any communication with a signalsman who was assigned to you or was with you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I read his statement, and I think he was trying to defend himself by shifting the buck to someone else. I don't remember that he talked to me, although I do remember all conversations. Maybe not in all details. But if he had talked to my signalsman while I was away in Orahovac, I believe that upon my return, my signalsman would have told me if Major Obrenovic had called. But since that didn't happen, I don't believe that he had in fact called. So I don't think that he actually talked to me on that day the way he put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you recall actually having inquired with your signalsman about any communications that may have occurred in your absence?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: There was no need for me to inquire, because whatever they received, whatever information they received, they would pass it on to the commander or whoever was in charge in the commander's absence. So there must have been nothing to report to me, because I don't believe he would have forgotten or omitted to let me know. And in fact, if I had talked to Major Obrenovic on the 14th, I would have had quite a few questions for him. But I don't remember we talked, especially since Major Obrenovic claimed that he didn't know anything about those events, although he later admitted that he did. And why would he have inquired with me, who knew nothing about all that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, having read his statement, were you aware that he made a reference to the term "Zoljani"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I believe that we're going way beyond the scope of what is supposed to be obtained as evidence in chief from this witness. This witness, we have a summary, he is supposed to testify about Orahovac. Now, in my cross-examination I do plan on getting into those areas, but I don't think it's the time now to ask questions about a statement that the witness might have read. The witness is here to testify as to what he knows, what he saw, and what he heard at that time, and not to testify as to what he heard, although I will in my cross-examination get into those areas. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. On the other hand, we still don't know what the question is going to be. So let's hear what -- hear the question first and then we'll -- we'll decide whether you have a point or not. Yes, could you repeat or finalise your question, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So far you've just referred the witness to the Obrenovic statement which according to you he makes reference to the term "Zoljani."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's my question in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you aware of that, is my question?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: The term "Zoljani" is familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just so that the record is clear, could you tell the Court what that term refers to?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Maybe it would be a good idea if you could read out to me that statement of his so that I could clarify. There are other ones except Zoljani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely we would stand in the way. Just restrict yourself, as you have already done, to putting to the witness the meaning of the term "Zoljani." And either you know what it means or you don't know what it means. You don't need to refer to anybody's statement in order to explain what Zoljani means. If you don't know what it means tell us you don't know. Say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Are you in a position to answer the President's question? Do you know what the term means?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Zoljani was an intervention platoon of our 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us where the intervention platoon was based?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: While we were at Baljkovica that platoon was based in a house near the command. When we were in Kitovnice they were again close to the command. When the command was at the beginning in Orahovac, they were once again close to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of whether or not Major Obrenovic made any statement relating to information that you had about Orahovac on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness is here to testify about what he heard, what he saw when he was on the ground in July 1995. Not a to what he knows whether there was a statement made or not. That's not what he's here for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment. I'll consult with my colleagues, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Objection sustained, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: You indicated that you had read Major Obrenovic's statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you indicated that your assessment of it was that maybe he was trying to shift the blame; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Same objection, Mr. President. That's not why the witness is here. The witness is here to testify about what he saw, what he heard in Orahovac, and I ask that my colleague be stopped from asking those questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I need to -- do you wish to respond to that, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do wish to respond to it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a little bit different from the previous question, but still there is a point that has been made by Mr. Bourgon that needs to be decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. If I may respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, there are two issues that are at play. First of all, it has to do with the witness's -- could I have the witness remove his headphones, because I think it would be inappropriate to make this argument in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But -- one moment. Ask him to put the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry about that. Ask him to put the headphones on again. Mr. Ristic, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You can now remove your headphones. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There are two points that I wish to raise. One is that we anticipate fully that the Defence intends to explore certain differences in the information that will be or has been related by Major Obrenovic as concerns the knowledge of this witness concerning the events of Orahovac on the 14th. I think Mr. Bourgon has alluded to that in his prior objection. Therefore, I think it is a relevant point to explore with the witness. The second reason that it's important is that to the extent that the witness perceives that statement as having been an attempt by a witness to be called by the Prosecution to shift the blame from himself or from someone else to this witness, it influences this witness's testimony and to that extent it is directly relevant to his credibility and the way to which his testimony or -- or the weight attributed to his testimony by the finder of fact. So I think on both grounds the -- the question is appropriately put, and the answer is both probative and material to this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, in reply to my colleague's arguments, the fact that some issue is likely to be raised during cross-examination doesn't make an issue relevant for examination-in-chief. The fact that the witness -- my colleague says that this might have an impact on the credibility of the witness, credibility during examination-in-chief is something for the Trial Chamber to examine and to assess, and credibility is something for the Defence, if the Defence wishes, to take or at least to challenge the credibility of the witness, then we can raise some issues. It's not for the Prosecution at this stage to raise issue, to challenge the credibility of his witness. Once again I recall that this witness was called to testify on precise issues. Those issues will arise soon. We have been given a summary, a Rule 65 ter summary. So far, we have not complained even though everything that has been said so far, none of it, is in the Rule 65 ter summary. Normally we would have objected to that because he's not supposed to go beyond the Rule 65 ter summary but we didn't complain because this witness is here and he's talking about things that he saw on the ground, that he perceived on the ground, that he heard on the ground. Now, for my colleague to get into his feeling concerning a statement of somebody else, that's not proper during examination-in-chief. So for all these reasons I simply ask that my colleague be stopped from asking these questions and we limit ourselves to the knowledge of the witness, what he had heard and what he saw in July of 1995, and whatever his relationship was with Major Obrenovic or with anybody else at that time, then that is correct, but for the rest he should be stopped. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I notice that you seem to indicate that in your opinion the -- to indicate that according to you the Prosecution at this stage is trying to challenge -- this is how it appears in the transcript: "It is not for the Prosecution at this stage to raise issue to challenge the credibility of his witness." I understood Mr. Vanderpuye to be doing exactly the opposite. I understood him to be making reference to statements by Obrenovic, putting them to the witness, particularly in the areas where Obrenovic supposedly tries to shift the responsibility from him onto the witness so that, through this series of questions and answers, the Prosecution will seek, rather, to uphold the credibility of the witness, rather, not challenge it. This is how I understand it. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, my reply was directed at what my colleague said at page 22, at lines 15 to 18, and may I cite from my colleague: "The second reason that it's important is that to the extent that the witness perceives the statement as having been an attempt by a witness to be called by the Prosecution to shift the blame from himself or from someone else to this witness, it influences this witness's testimony and to that extent it is directly relevant to his credibility." That's not what we're trying to get during examination-in-chief. During examination-in-chief, we're trying to get what the witness knows and what he has -- what he has heard and what he has seen when he was in July of 1995 with -- in his capacity as commander of the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Final -- thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Final remarks from you very briefly, Mr. Vanderpuye, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Very briefly, I think my colleague's arguments while maybe well-intended is not well-guided. I think it is entirely up to the trier of fact to have the opportunity to put in context the testimony of a witness who is before it, whose credibility and the weight to which it will attach certain things is critical. And I don't think that the Prosecution should be put in a position of putting an automaton on the stand and pressing a button and playback, rather to present to the Trial Chamber a complete picture of the witness so that the Trial Chamber can make a well-founded assessment as to the weight to attach to this witness's testimony, and indeed in this case to the extent that involves a future Prosecution witness the weight to attach that witness's testimony as well. So it's entirely relevant to the proceedings, it is entirely relevant to the matter at issue which is the subject matter of the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. The whole point as I see it now I will confer with my colleagues. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Your Honours. First off, we would join Mr. Bourgon's argument, but secondly I'm a little confused. Is the

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: (redacted) One of them is got to be not speaking the truth from what I hear coming from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Let me confer --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Meek has just posed the question that I think is essential to this debate. I think Mr. Vanderpuye needs to address the question: Is he attacking the credibility of his own witness now or is he seeking to bolster it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Usually we allow -- when there are more than one counsel -- is there any objection on the Defence side to give the floor to Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You have to remain silent, Mr. McCloskey. Perhaps while -- while we are conferring you may confer with Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we've come to -- one moment, because I was marking something here, and I forgot what it was now. We have decided as follows: We uphold the objection by Mr. Bourgon -- or from Mr. Bourgon, and we direct you as follows: That you put to the witness questions which will elicit his version of events, events that others may be testifying upon but reference only to the events and not to possible evidence by other people. That's number one. And secondly, of course, your rights to put further questions on redirect, if that's the case, are being saved. So that's the position. He needs -- he understood me. Okay. Thank you for being patient with us, Witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. What I had wanted to say just before you decided this issue, and I don't think it's an issue that concerns -- is that the Prosecution's position is that we feel that it would be appropriate for the Court just to be aware that there are at times differences in the testimony of witnesses and that's the reason why it was raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I mean, we are familiar to the same kind -- we are familiar to the same kind of procedure. I know -- practically all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If the credibility of this witness is attacked on cross-examination, you have every opportunity to put further questions on redirect to counter -- counteract that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. That's no problem there. All right. Okay. Thank you for bearing with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You remember the events of the 14th of July, 1995, you'd indicated previously; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you at some point during that day become aware of certain things going on in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: On the 14th of July, the afternoon, a soldier from the 2nd Company of my battalion came looking for me. He was originally from Orahovac. He asked me what was going on in Orahovac, that I didn't want to talk to them about what was going on. They had heard from a soldier who went to Orahovac via Potocari [as interpreted]. He went to the upper portion of Orahovac, and he saw there a large number of people assembled by the school in Orahovac. The soldier who came looking for me, the one who was from the 2nd Company, told me, "We want to abandon our positions and go and defend our wives and children." I told him that I would verify what was going on, that I was unaware of anything, and that I would get back to them, and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recall the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry to interrupt but this time I wait until the witness finished his answer. I believe he said Potocani and not Potocari. It makes a difference, Potocani is close to the area of Baljkovica, and I think we can clarify with the witness he said Potocani and not Potocari. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ristic, you have heard what Mr. Bourgon has just stated, that you had mentioned Potocani and not Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a village near Baljkovica, a Muslim village, that was destroyed, and it's called either Potocari or Potocani. You can see it on the map. I'm not sure if it's an R or an N.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So but -- but let's make this clear. Previously in answering Mr. Vanderpuye's question you said, "On the 14th of July, the afternoon, a soldier from the 2nd Company of my battalion came looking for me. He was originally from Orahovac. He asked me what was going on in Orahovac, that I didn't want to talk to them about what was going on. They had heard from a soldier who went to Orahovac via," or via Potocari or Potocani. This is the small -- whatever the name is, this is the small Muslim village that had been destroyed. Is this what you're referring to? Or were you referring to Potocari, the town that you referred to earlier on in your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to the village near Baljkovica, a small village that was destroyed, and it's called Potocani if the other place is called Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Mr. Vanderpuye. I think it's clear enough now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think I was about to ask you what the name of the soldier was who sought you on the 14th. Do you recall his name?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us what it is, please?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: He called me on the phone from the positions. He didn't come looking for me personally. He called me on the phone from his trench where his company was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall his name?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Jovo Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you indicated that you would look into this matter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you just tell us what you did in order to look into this matter?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: The first thing I did was to call the duty service in the brigade. I asked them what was going on in Orahovac. They told me, "Just do your work. This is no business of yours."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recall who he spoke to at the duty service, as you've indicated?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I didn't recognise the voice. I asked for Major Obrenovic, and he told me that he was in Snagovo sector. I didn't recognise the voice, and I don't think that I spoke to that person any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when you say "duty service," and perhaps it's a translation issue, are you referring to it a duty officer or duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: The duty service within the brigade had a duty operations officer and an assistant. They were located near all of the offices of the operations service and near the commander. So it is possible that one of those people answered the phone and that the duty officer had gone out, or perhaps that was the deputy of the duty officer. I didn't really care who answered the phone, because I called the brigade command. And it couldn't have been just anybody from the street sitting in the office of the duty service. It could have been only one of the officers working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know who was assigned as the duty operations officer at that time or the duty officer that day?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I know that that evening Major Jokic, who was the duty officer, called me. He inquired about the situation in the battalion and told me that large columns of Muslims from Srebrenica were on their way towards Baljkovica, that we should take care. I know that Jokic called me that evening. I knew his voice. But on that day it wasn't him, definitely not him. I knew him because he's from the same town as I am, and he frequently called to inquire about the situation precisely because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So you -- okay. Now, I think you indicated that you asked for Major Obrenovic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you able to find out where he was?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: The duty officer conveyed to me that he was in the Snagovo sector and that he was busy intercepting those columns. I understood that he wasn't available, and I stopped asking to speak to him. And the reason I called in was to inquire about what was going on. Then I told my people that I would check what was going on, that they should not leave their positions. And I called a civilian from Orahovac who worked in a shop to inquire with her whether she knew what was going on by the school in Orahovac. She told me that prisoners had been brought to the school and that one of our soldiers from our battalion who was from Orahovac, that the prisoners grabbed a rifle from him and that the security men managed to get the situation under control and avoid any incidents. Following that, Major -- or, rather, Captain Trbic called me saying that -- asking, rather, to send him a dozen people to assist with the -- with providing security at the school because the prisoners were about to break out from the school. I did as he asked. I called the people on the positions, telling them that some prisoners had arrived there and that I had sent a dozen people or so to assist with the security around the school so as to avoid the prisoners from breaking out and dispersing throughout the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think this is a good point to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, Mr. Ristic. You'd indicated that you'd made a phone call to an individual who told you about prisoners being brought to the school. Just so the record is clear, could you tell us who that person is?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Mara Matic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You also indicated that she mentioned something about one of the prisoners or prisoners having grabbed a rifle from a soldier from your battalion. Can you tell us who that soldier was, if you know?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Gojko Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us what Mr. Simic's position was in your battalion?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic had been the commander of the Orahovac Company for a long time before he was replaced at his own request due to some personal problems he had, and from that time on he was a regular soldier in the 2nd Company of the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, were you aware that Mr. Simic was in the vicinity of the school on the 14th of July? Were you aware that he was there prior to that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: No, I was not. The first time I heard about it was from that woman. She told me that he was there, but he had been absent from the 1st to the 15th of July because he needed to see his son off to the army. And along with him another eight members of the 4th Battalion were absent for the same reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, the other eight members of the 4th Battalion, do you know whether or not any of those members were in and around the area of the school in Orahovac on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I don't know that any of them were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know if someone by the name of Risto Trifkovic, first, was in your battalion, and, second, if he was in the area of Orahovac on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I don't know where he was, but I think he was supposed to be with the battalion. It all depends on what his deployment was. I don't know where Trifkovic was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I just note that the Prosecution is asking questions according to a name, Risto Trifkovic; first time we hear this name. Whether in all the statements that were provided by this witness or the Rule 65 ter summaries or anything in the indictment or anything in the pre-trial brief, first time we hear this name. If the Prosecution has information concerning this individual it would be nice if it could be disclosed to the Defence counsel before a question is asked of a witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your comments, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like to defer to my colleague, Mr. McCloskey, to answer this question with the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is different. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And out of an abundance of caution, it's probably best that the witness take his headphones off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Witness. Mr. Ristic. Mr. Ristic. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We -- we have -- you may recall the testimony of an Orahovac survivor who spoke of recognising the voice of Gojko Simic. It's a long time ago, but -- and you may recall the evidence where that survivor had heard the -- Gojko Simic referring to someone as Risto and someone as Vojo. So all we're doing here is bringing out that there are people with that first name in his battalion, and I will endeavour to see if there -- we do have some statements from these folks, at least one of them, that we should have provided the Defence. We will make sure that we have or, if we haven't, we will do it at the break. And -- but this is just merely to determine that the identity of -- to remind us that there were these two first names that were mentioned to show that there were people with those first names in that battalion. That's all that this is for, but we will provide statements because they do -- I don't think they -- they may not agree with the survivor of being there. I don't recall exactly, but we'll check and make sure we give that to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if I understood Mr. Bourgon well, it's the combination of the name and surname that he's referring to, not just the existence of a Risto, but also this Risto being Risto Trifkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, but we, of course, didn't want to just ask the witness if -- there was this person by the name of a first -- just the first name, so we gave the full name just so it was -- made more sense, and so the statement that the Defence has makes more sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I don't think this question arises off-the-cuff. Was the name of Risto Trifkovic put to the witness when he was being proofed already, or -- no. I see Mr. Vanderpuye denying that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Indeed I was shaking my head. No, the name wasn't put to the witness previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Bourgon, do you wish to add anything? At this stage I don't think it's case but --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I just think they should tell us in advance if they're going to try to do something with the witness. This we're taken by surprise once again, and we don't feel it's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I assume even the witness is being taken by surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can't choreograph every detail and this -- these, Risto and Vojo, have been part of the history of this case for many years, as has the Orahovac Company roster. So this is not a mystery and this is -- there's nothing new here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The understanding is, if you have dug up fresh information that points to a certain Risto Trifkovic, then you will pass on the information to the Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and we should have done that if we haven't, and I agree with Mr. Bourgon on that and I will double-check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. And Mr. Vanderpuye, do you -- yeah, but anyway, the question has been put and he has answered it already, so I don't know what -- whether you -- if it's the case of proceeding with another question on this or whether to proceed with some other question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As you can imagine, I have a question relating to the Vojo part of the Risto --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- so I would ask if the witness could put his headphones back on. Okay. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you have somebody by the name of Vojo Matic in your battalion?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I think he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You think he was there. Where?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: In the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know if he was in the area in and around Orahovac on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I had no knowledge about the whereabouts of that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to Gojko Simic, did you ever have an opportunity to discuss with him his whereabouts on the 14th at a later time?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Gojko Simic got killed near the battalion command on the 15th or the 16th. At any rate, he'd got killed. So I had no occasion to talk to him. I would have probably discussed those matters with him, but as I said, he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, I think you had, before the break, indicated that you had received a call from Milorad Trbic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you just tell us the circumstances surrounding that call and what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: He only requested assistance in the form of ten men, and he said the prisoners were about to break out from the schoolhouse. I didn't ask him anything else, and he didn't tell me anything else. My understanding was that there were prisoners in the schoolhouse and that the place needed security, and without knowing exactly how many there were or what the problem was, I sent some men there, some men that had been busy in ambushes during the night and were at the command during the day. The order had come from the command, and I must have been the first, the closest person around, so he requested that assistance from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did he convey to you that the order had come from the command during that -- during that telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: He didn't tell me anything except what I've just described, and I didn't ask him anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So as far as you're concerned, was this a direct order from Mr. Trbic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: It didn't sound like an order. It was a request for assistance. He didn't issue me an order. He told me to send him 10 men to help out with the prisoners who were about to break out from the school. I sent my men and called up those people there, telling them that I would keep in touch and tell them what's going on, and that I had sent 10 men for assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye. After you received this communication or after you received this request from Mr. Trbic, were you free to say no to him and not make available any of your men? Could you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know what was going to be done, and I didn't ask. I only assumed that some prisoners had been brought and that security was needed. Maybe I could have done otherwise, but I sent those men in order to secure that front end of the line which was much more important to me. If he had told me that my men were needed for executions, I would probably have done differently. But in actual fact, he told me that they were needed to provide security, because those men were taken out from trenches where they were defending the defence line to help out with another activity related to ambushes, and they were also able to help with security, to secure those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you just tell us of the 10 men that you sent there, where were they taken from, because you've indicated that they were in some trenches and also -- or engaged in activity related to ambushes. What area were they drawn from?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: They were taken from companies that were deployed on the front end of the defence line. They were taken out from trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I see in relation to the Judge's question about whether or not you had a choice, just so that we're clear on this, was the answer to that yes or no? And that's with respect to the men that you were asked to send.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: It's not that I had a choice, but in practice we helped each other out in all kinds of situations. If somebody was under attack and was short of men and we had enough to lend some, we would do so. But that particular situation was happening for the first time. I didn't actually know what was going on. He told me he needed men for security service, and I sent some men to report to Captain Trbic. I wasn't thinking at that moment about -- there was just that call. I wasn't thinking about any choices. Everything would have been different if he had told me that some executions were involved, but he just told me they were needed for security duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the men that you withdrew from the line to send to Captain Trbic, did you have a plan in place to replace these men or were there other men available from other locations to fill those vacated positions?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Through communications I sent a message to company commanders that an order had arrived saying that a platoon should be formed because there was no intervention platoon. We had some surplus of personnel. In some trenches there were four or five men, and if on some other end people were sick or absent, they would be shifted. If we needed to raise the level of readiness or alertness, we would put in a new trench where needed. And as we sent assistance to others, others would send personnel to us when we needed it, when our own men were on sick leave or absent for other reasons. And those people could always return to the defence line anyway because they were close to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In fact, at the time that you sent these 10 men to Captain Trbic, was that after the men from the 3rd Infantry had been dispatched to the area of Snagovo? These were the men that were securing your mortar platoon. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So is it -- is it the case that you'd assign these 10 men to Captain Trbic without anybody to secure your mortar platoon in the afternoon of the 14th?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Activities unfolded in such a way that our mortar platoon was not in danger on the 14th. If they had been in jeopardy, probably they would have been given some assistance, but the way it was, not knowing how things were developing at various locations, I did what I did. And later on in the evening of the 14th, I was making a new plan, feeling that there might be some danger, because I had already received information that they had crossed Crni Vrh. So I was going to boost the security of our defence line against members of the army coming from Srebrenica and other BH army troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Did you at any point share this concern with Captain Trbic when he made the request for these 10 men, or you didn't share that with him at all?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I didn't talk to him at all. I probably would have talked to him if I had found him in Orahovac when I was there, but I saw that he was leaving that place, going off somewhere on a truck. I had nobody else there to ask any questions, but I could see what was going on. My men were gathered on the pitch outside that gym, and they were so scared that all they could ask was whether I would let them go home, because before that I had suggested they return to the battalion, and they wanted instead to go home and report back at the battalion at 8.00 a.m. the next morning. I realised that could create a wave of panic at the battalion, so I let them go home and told them they needed to return to the battalion to get involved again in our activities to boost security of the defence line we were keeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this since you've indicated that you actually went to Orahovac and -- could you just share with the Court how it is that you came to be there and why it is that you went? But first let me ask you, why is it you went to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I got a telephone call from one of those 10 soldiers. I can't remember which one, but I think I assigned one of them to be the leader of that group because that was the common practice when a group of men were absenting themselves. They had to keep in touch. He told me they were asking us to execute some people. What shall we do? I said, "Don't do anything. I'm coming." I came to Orahovac with a driver, and they all gathered around me. That's how the conversation went as far as that issue is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you just tell us about how long after you had sent these men down to Orahovac that you received this call?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to remember after all this time. Certainly some time had elapsed, but I can't tell you exactly. A certain time elapsed from when they called me. I really can't be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's all right. Can you -- can you tell us about what time of day it was that you got this call around -- and how long after, say, you sent the men down after you received the call?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: All that was going on in the afternoon of the 14th. I can guess now, but I really can't give you a precise answer, because I didn't keep my eye on the clock. All that was going on on the 14th in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In response to the call that you got, I think you said that you told them that -- "Don't do anything. I'm coming." Did you inquire as to who was ordering them to participate in these executions?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I did not inquire about anything. If Captain Trbic had been there I would have probably inquired of him and talked to him, but since he wasn't there, I couldn't find any of the other officers that I would like to speak to. And I was both irritated and angry over Trbic's absence, because he had asked assistance from me and then took off himself. So as things were, I tried to return to my own base in Baljkovica where my battalion was deployed and get it over with.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, just before we get there, let me ask you, did you -- perhaps my question wasn't clear, but during the course of the conversation that you had with your men about being ordered to participate in the executions, did you ask them anything at all about the circumstances of that order?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask them anything really. They were regular soldiers. I wasn't aware that they knew any of those officers anyway, and I made no inquiries. I just did what I told you I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is there any particular reason why you didn't ask anything?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Most likely the events themselves, because if somebody wants you to give them people for one task and when you went there and you see that it actually involves another task, something quite different, then upon realising this I wanted to pull out my people so that they wouldn't participate in it, because we had our regular task to hold the defence lines and not to deal with those issues. This is why I did not even inquire about those events, because that wasn't part of my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could you describe for us -- well, you've indicated first that you went to Orahovac with a driver. Could you just tell us who -- what his name is, please?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: The driver within the Medical Corps, Lazar Matic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what vehicle you took in order to reach Orahovac from your location?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: It was a car that belonged to the battalion Medical Corps, a Lada vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how long did it take you from the time you left until the time you -- left the battalion until the time you arrived in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Ten to 15 minutes. About 15 minutes, maybe even more. It depends on how you drive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you leave word with anybody at the time that you left as to where you would be and how you could be reached?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Most likely I spoke only to signalsman, and if somebody was present in the headquarters I might have said to one of the members of the command that I was on my way to Orahovac and would stay there only briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could just refer you to the time that you arrived at Orahovac. Could you just tell us as particularly as you can what you first observed when you entered that area?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: When I came near the school building I saw a lot of people there. There were security men there, people with rifles, and then there were also civilians just watching it. Then there were cars parked between the road leading to Kitovnice and Zvornik. So between the main road and the playground there were a lot of cars parked. There were soldiers, civilians, a mix and match type of gathering without any sense or organisation. It was mostly people simply observing what was going on rather than doing anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you at some point arrive at the school itself?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you indicated earlier that you saw Captain Trbic in a truck or getting into a truck. Could you just describe for us where that -- where you saw him first?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: When I reached the edge of the playground along the road leading to Zvornik and some hundred metres later on that road I saw Trbic and two military policemen getting on a truck, which was a cross between a truck and Tamic, but it was a civilian vehicle. And I saw the vehicle depart in that direction towards Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, the two military policemen that you say you saw, do you happen to know who they are?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I think that they were lawyers in the military police. Goran Bogdanovic and Cedo Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What happened after -- let me ask you this first, I'm sorry: When you made this observation were you in your vehicle or outside of your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: We stopped there. Now, whether I was still in the vehicle or had gone out earlier, I don't know. I was out of the vehicle and the driver had gone to park the car. I know that I saw it. Now, whether I saw it while I was still in the car or once I got out of the car, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: After you made this observation, what's the next thing that you did?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I started towards the playground. When those people saw me, they approached the area around the gym, or I don't know whether they had been there already earlier. But at any rate, they were there. They assembled. I told them to line up. They lined up in a line, and we started a conversation. They wanted to go home. They looked scared, and I let them go.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just so that the record is clear, can you tell us who these people are that you're talking about just now that looked scared, that came towards you in the area of the playground?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: It's very hard to remember who those people were because the battalion numbered 450 men. They were gone for two days only, and on the third day they came back to their trenches. It's very hard to remember the names, especially given the passage of time. I can't remember the names of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. But these are the men that you sent you're talking about; right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you inquire of these men who was in charge or who was in command in this area at the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I talked to them. However, since I saw that there was the military police commander there, then Trbic, and that there were other people from the military police there, too, I most likely looked for Drago Nikolic there. However, since he wasn't there or I didn't find him, there was no need for me to look for anybody else or to remain there longer. Since I had let those people go, I returned to the battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
