utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I don't recall if he specified the approximate time when he arrived to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think that's a reasonable concern. I'll put it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, if you can recall, approximately what -- around what time you arrived at the -- at the school?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact time, but it was most likely late in the afternoon. I could give you an approximate time, but I don't know if it's accurate because I didn't look at my watch to see what time it was. I can't be fully precise, but I can give you an approximate time. It could have been 4.00 p.m., 5.00 p.m., maybe 3.00 p.m. I can't remember because I didn't look at my watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicated that you most likely looked for Drago Nikolic there. I think that's what you said. And when you say you -- you most likely looked for him, what do you recall having done in order to find him, if anything at all?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I didn't do anything, nor was I supposed to do anything. I needed somebody to complain to them, because they had asked for people to help with the security. Maybe they even invented the story themselves because they simply wanted to go home. Though things happened, you know. People fabricated stories because they wanted to leave their positions and go home. However, I failed to find him and I didn't find anybody else. I don't know what else to tell you. I didn't find anyone else. I didn't look for anybody else, I didn't need anyone else because I wasn't in charge, nor was I doing what I was supposed to be doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recall if anybody had mentioned to you whether or not Mr. Nikolic was there or had been there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that accurately because there was a lot of noise, a lot of commotion there. It was a long time ago. There are only two possibilities. Based on the fact that I saw people from the brigade security there, it means I was either looking for him, or perhaps one of them told me that, but I can't say whether they did and, if they did, whether it was accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If I read back to your -- read back your prior statement to you, do you think that would help you -- help you recall whether or not somebody had mentioned to you that Mr. Nikolic had been there? Would that help you in any way?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I know what I stated last time in my statement, and I don't think it would be of assistance to me. I've been thinking about it for a long period of time, and I really can't remember the circumstances under which I was looking for him. I simply can't remember that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, since you remember what you stated, would you share that with the Court?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I said that it was possible that one of those people said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. One moment. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My colleague is making reference to a statement. At the beginning he started and he said that the witness had three opportunities to meet people. I'd like to know which statement my colleague is referring to, because the witness has to know what statement. Is it the first one that he gave, the second one, or is it the interview with the Prosecution when he was worked upon to say something else? Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough, because I think the witness himself knows exactly which statement is being referred to, but the Defence have a right to know exactly which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do agree with the Court's analysis. However, I think that -- I'm not actually referring the witness to a statement. The witness has indicated that he remembers independently of any reference that I've made to a statement that he made, and I'm simply asking him to share with us what that statement is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which statement are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I couldn't know until he answers the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So, Witness -- yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, my colleague is not saying exactly. He said, and I look at page 47, lines 22 to 23rd, and he said: "Well, since you remember what you stated, would you share that with the Court?" I'm saying, stated when and how, so that the witness knows what my colleague is talking about. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is also a point in what Mr. Vanderpuye said, that maybe there has been more than one instance when the witness referred to what he was just about starting to relate to us. So let's hear what he has to say first, and then I think we can specify to -- specify which statement or one or more he's referring -- he himself is referring to. So, Witness, let me read out to you six lines from the transcript. You had said: "I know what I stated last time in my statement, and I don't think it would be of assistance to me. I've been thinking about it for a long period of time, and I really can't remember the circumstances under which I was looking for him. I simply can't remember that at all." And then Mr. Vanderpuye suggested that since you remember what you stated, perhaps you could share that with us. And before you were interrupted, you just started telling us, and according to the transcript you said: "I said that it was possible that one of those people said ..." Will you continue from there, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This information would be complete had I seen Mr. Nikolic there. However, since I didn't see him, and I don't know why I was looking for him - that's how it happened - after all this time has passed I couldn't say whether it was because the members of the brigade military police were there or whether one of those people present said that Drago was there. I can't say which way it was. If I knew the man who told me that I would have been able to prove this. But the essence of what I'm saying, if you allow me to give an explanation is this: When I gave that first statement to the Zvornik MUP about the events, I was told this was a statement for a commission established by the government of the Republika Srpska because Major Obrenovic had mentioned me in his statement. So I gave that first statement. My second statement was given to the security organs from Bijeljina, and in it I said that I would clarify to the commission of the government of Republika Srpska, which had been established to investigate the events in Srebrenica, that I was going to clarify to them some details from my Zvornik statement, and this is why that statement is not perhaps fully precise for the purposes of this court. This statement given in Banja Luka, I don't know where it was, was suppose to be expanded in order to clarify all these details. As for the events in Orahovac, whatever I said was true, and I can't deviate from what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. You indicated that there were some people from the military police that you saw. Can you tell us who it is that you saw?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I saw commander of the military police company walking on the road. I saw a member of the military police, Nada Stevanovic [as interpreted]. I knew her. She was carrying water in a bucket. And then there was some other policemen there. I didn't try to remember them. I saw that they acted as security there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did you see any other officers from where -- well, from where you were?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: As I stood in the middle of the playground with my people, I saw by the road a car, a civilian car. I think it was a Lada. I also saw a young man with one or two stripes, either second lieutenant or lieutenant, with two soldiers opening a trunk and taking out an 84-millimetre machine-gun. That's what I saw as I stood there. Later on, I didn't really pay attention. I didn't look to see where they went and what they did. I simply saw this by chance as I stood there and observed what was going on around the playground, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, can I have the last name of that lady, Nada? The transcript says Stevanovic, but it may be different.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it is Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ristic, could you tell me the last name of Nada?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The transcript said Stevanovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Judge. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Can I just ask you if you could tell us what the name of the military police commander that you saw around, what his name was?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Military police company commander Miomir Jasikovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And at the time what you observed Commander Jasikovac, can you tell us what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Walking on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And where was he?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: At the end of the playground next to the road going from Zvornik to Kitovnice, by the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you at any time during the period of time that you were at the school converse with Mr. Jasikovac?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the individual you saw you indicated had two stripes. Did you recognise that individual as a member of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I think that he was on the side -- or, rather, I think that he was from outside. I knew people from the brigade. He definitely was not from the Zvornik Brigade. He was from elsewhere, but I don't know anything else about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is he the same individual that you saw handling this machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: He didn't have it. He simply stood by the car while the two soldiers were getting it out. Why they were getting it out, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you see any vehicles in and around the -- the school?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: In that area between the Zvornik-Kitovnice road and the playground there were about a dozen cars parked, among them a van. I think that mostly those were civilian cars. I didn't pay particular attention to them, but I think they were mostly civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you see any military vehicles in the vicinity of the school, that is, close to the school itself?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you see any trucks as aside from cars, for example?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I saw a green Tamic, two tonne or so. It was parked behind my back, in the middle of the gym going into reverse, and it had a tarpaulin cover on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you able to determine whether there was anybody inside, other than I guess the driver, but anybody in the back part of the truck at the time that you observed it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I didn't pay attention. I saw it arrive, and I saw it go into reverse and park while I was standing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you able to see where it had come from, what -- from which direction or location?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I think it arrived from the direction of Kitovnice, on that road, but that's questionable, even though most likely that's how it was because I was able to see as I stood there. I was facing the road. I think it arrived empty from that direction. It parked there. And I didn't ask about anything, why or where.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you -- did you gain any information as to where it was that these prisoners were being held, or did you see them out and about at the time that you arrived at the school?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I didn't see them move about, but when I finished with my men I went to look for my driver and the car to go back to the battalion. I started following Nada to see to whom she was carrying the water, and I saw her carrying the water towards the school. There was another door between the school and the gym, and I saw that there were prisoners inside. I simply looked inside and went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to whether or not the truck was used for the purposes of loading these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Probably. I didn't put any questions, but probably so. I could have supposed what was being done, because when I approached -- when one approached, one could see what was going on. So I didn't inquire. I didn't investigate anything. I simply saw this and went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, when you say one could see what was going on, could you just describe it maybe briefly what it is that you saw?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: On my way back to the battalion I saw at that fork off near the fountain that there were some people parked there, some security people. And outside the school itself it was very noisy. Clamour outside, clamour inside. That's all I could see, but I didn't look for anything in particular. I wasn't interested. I didn't see any details. That's what I could see on my way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On your way were you able to see if there were any soldiers away from the school in or around the main road?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I can't recall all the details, but there were some walking on the road. Some were standing. I can't tell you precisely who was where.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers off the main road and away from the school?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see, there were some soldiers standing off the road near that fountain as we were passing through on our way to Baljkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us from what you observed of these soldiers what, if anything, they were doing?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I suppose they were there as security detail, or maybe they came to watch. I think they were security, but I wasn't really there in order to know who was in charge of what.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At the time that you -- you've indicated that you at some point sent your men home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, having done that, did you notify the battalion that you had taken that action?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: When I came to the battalion I convened all the members of the command and told them that there was a danger looming over our battalion. I told them what was going on down there. I told them that I let some men go home, that they would be coming back the next day, and I agreed with the other members of my command that that evening we should transport the vehicles, ammunition, et cetera, to the area of Parlici [phon]. We agreed that a group of our guards would go to an elevation called Remic hill overlooking the command, and from that vantage point they would observe and look out for that group if it comes into view moving towards the command. If it should be a smaller group, we would engage them in combat, and if they should be a larger group, we would retreat to the front end of our defence line and open the way for them simply to save the lives of our battalion if we are unable to fight them. And that's what the plan was until the next day, the 15th, when Major Obrenovic came to the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, at the time that you withdrew your men from the school, did you notify anybody at the school that you were withdrawing them from the security detail?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I did not tell anyone anything, because I didn't see any of the officers. I did what I did. Why, I really don't know. If Trbic had been there, it would have been different. I would have talked to him. But as it was, I knew there was no brigade commander, no chief of staff, no one else I could complain to, and I thought I was acting in the best interests of my men.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you at any time -- while you were still at the school, did you at any time seek to contact the brigade as distinguished from the battalion?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: No. I told you already what I did. I didn't look for anyone, and I didn't find anyone. I simply didn't want to get involved, and that's why I acted the way I did, because my job was in the battalion, not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You indicated earlier in your testimony that you were somewhat upset with Captain Trbic. Could you tell us why that was the case? And that is on the 14th when you went down to the school.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I think I answered that question, too, when I told you that that man had asked me for assistance while going off himself. And I felt cheated. I was angry because of that, because asking someone else for assistance while running away yourself is something that I think was really wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Following these events did you have an opportunity to speak to Captain Trbic about this particular circumstance that you were upset about?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I had no opportunity to talk to him because after those events, after the 14th, there were two days of fighting in which we had great losses. We had lost a lot of men. The command base was set on fire. We needed to rebuild the command, and I simply had no occasion to talk to him. But apart from that, I don't think anyone was very eager to discuss it anyway. I continued with my own activities because it was not my job to investigate or inquire. My job was in the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to speak to your commander when he returned about the -- about the events of the 14th?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I told him everything that had happened in his absence. And when he returned, we continued our activities related to the establishment of the command of the 4th Battalion. First they were under tents, and later on we placed our command into a prefab building and continued our activities within the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have an opportunity to discuss this with the brigade commander, Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic at the time?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I talked to the brigade commander on the 15th of July, in the afternoon, late afternoon, when he called me up. I was having some problems with my mortar platoon when Commander Pandurevic called me up and told me not to worry, he was there. He was just trying to encourage me because he knew that I had no combat experience, that my commander was absent, that I was practically on my own. And I felt better to hear that he was back, and when he told me that he had sent one platoon from the 7th Battalion to reinforce our line of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you discuss with Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic the circumstances of the 14th involving what occurred at Orahovac at any time following the 14th or on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Did you discuss the circumstances surrounding the events of the 14th with Drago Nikolic at any time following the 14th or on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Not on the 14th and not later. But after a while, although I can't tell you precisely when, on one occasion I asked him why those detainees had been brought to Orahovac, to the school building, because it was dangerous, dangerous for the defence line and dangerous for the village and our entire battalion up there, because it was obvious in that column broke through there would go through Krizevacke Njive and Baljkovica. And he said he had been told just to place them in the schoolhouse pending an exchange in Batkovici. I didn't ask him anything about other circumstances, and he didn't volunteer any information himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, did he explain to you how it is that these prisoners came to be in that school building?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I did not inquire about the details, and he didn't volunteer any details. In fact, I wasn't really interested. I just told him and Obrenovic the same thing: Why on earth were they brought to Orahovac? It's dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to your conversation with Obrenovic, did you receive a response to that question?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: His response was that he didn't know anything about those events, and I believed him when he said that it was all done along some security chain of command, not through the Main Staff. Later on, though, he admitted he had some knowledge about that, those activities, but at that time he said he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just bear with me for one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you indicated I think it was on the 15th that you spoke with Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic. First of all, is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And at the time that you spoke to the Lieutenant Colonel, do you know where Major Obrenovic was?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: He was with me at the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you recall when it is that he returned from the field to the command?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Major Obrenovic, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: He came to the command of the 4th Battalion between 1300 and 1400 hours on the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And did you have occasion to have a conversation with him regarding the events concerning the 14th at that time?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I couldn't talk to him, because before his arrival we were engaged in combat. There was an attack on the front end on our defence line that lasted that whole day. The attack start at 4.30 a.m. We had great losses, a lot of men killed and wounded. And when he came to the battalion, he didn't ask he me what the situation was like. He just asked me to provide him with one man. He was taking with him the intervention platoon of the 2nd Infantry Battalion, and they needed one man from me to take them to a point of about 2 to 300 metres above Potocani. And then another two platoons came from the Bratunac Brigade, he told me, and he wanted another man from me to take them to that area overlooking the command. And I understood that he was there to help with the defence of the battalion. In the meantime, the Praga arrived. The commander of the Drina Wolves detachment came with Major Obrenovic, and all the later developments concentrate on the defence of the command post all the way until the 16th at noon. So we really had our hands full and a lot of problems, and I don't remember discussing those events. I don't think we even had time to discuss those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you at any point between the 14th and, say, the 16th discuss with Major Obrenovic the assignment of the individuals he'd requested of you on the -- I believe it was on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: We didn't discuss that at all. Everything was focussed on the defence of the command, and there was no talk and no need to talk about anything else, because we were really in grave danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, thank you very much, Mr. Ristic. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. He hasn't told us how long he was at the school. In other words, how much time elapsed between his arrival and his departure from the school area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I will put that to him. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Ristic, can you tell it us about how long it was that you were in the school from the time you arrived until the time that you departed?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: My visit at that part of Orahovac lasted all of about 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear, could you tell us how long you were actually away from the command about, from the time that you left until the time that you returned?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult to say that precisely. Maybe it took 15 minutes by car. I stayed there for about 10 minutes. Then the time it took me to get back. All in all less than an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have you, Mr. Bourgon and you, Mr. Haynes both requesting two and a half hours for cross-examination. Have you come to an agreement amongst yourselves as to who is going first?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it would be the right moment to take the break at this stage in order to have a full session and also to reorganise because we had been informed that the examination-in-chief would be no more than one hour and now we need to reorganise in terms of who will go first and how we're going to work with this witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will find the cooperation of the Trial Chamber there. And again, I mean it was anticipated to -- the examination-in-chief was anticipated to last an hour and a half. It has almost lasted three hours. So I'm not chastising you, Mr. Vanderpuye, but almost. So we'll have a 25-minute break now, and then Mr. Bourgon or Mr. Haynes will commence the first cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see it's Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Bourgon, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we better tell the witness who you are. Mr. Bourgon is appearing for Nikolic here, Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ristic. Following the examination-in-chief which was conducted by my colleague, I have less questions than anticipated to ask you, so I'll move straight to my first topic, and that first topic refers to the actions which you took upon receiving the orders from Major Obrenovic on the 12th of July to put together an intervention platoon to go to Tisova Kosa. Do you recall testifying to that effect?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This platoon was put together, from my understanding of your testimony, was put together from soldiers that were picked from your three infantry companies that belonged to the 4th Battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as you mention, you detached someone from your command who had more experience to accompany this platoon to Tisova Kosa?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, we move to the 14th of July in the morning, and you said that on that day you received information that the intervention platoon from the 3rd Battalion had arrived to provide security for your mortar platoon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this platoon which had arrived, do you know who gave the orders or how were you informed that this platoon had arrived?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: They informed me from the brigade command that the platoon of the 3rd Infantry Battalion was coming to assist the mortar platoon and that they were it at the Motovo juncture. And then I went straight there and got into contact with the commander of that platoon. We distributed code signals to be part of the same radio network. I told him to deploy above Krizevacke Njive in the direction of Grujici where our mortars were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I recall from your testimony, you said that on the morning of the 14th of July, you received orders from Major Obrenovic to send this same platoon to the area of Snagovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that you did not get those instructions personally on the radio, but those were communicated to you by your signalman?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: The practice was that something like a telegram would be sent towards us. The signalsman from the brigade would pass it on to our signalsman who would enter it into a logbook, whether it was an order or just an information, and that was the practice we followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ristic. Now, just for clarification, when you say you received a telegram, can you confirm for the benefit of the Chamber you don't actually receive a piece of paper but actually the signalman receives verbal instructions that he writes down and then passes those to you, and this is what we mean by receiving a telegram. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was communicated by radio, not by courier, or it would be passed on in direct conversation between somebody from the brigade command and somebody from the battalion command. Orders and information could be passed that way, too, if it concerned our battalion, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And again for the sake of clarification, when we say "battalion command," just so that everybody understands, because I know it's a term that can be confusing, because sometimes other armies use the term "headquarters." So when you say "command," you're actually talking about the headquarters of your battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And within the command of the 4th Battalion there was no machine which would allow you to receive something in writing from the brigade command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: There was no machine. Only a courier could bring some written order from the brigade to our battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I move to when you received that order from Major Obrenovic on the 14th in the morning, my understanding is that at that point you have no knowledge whatsoever of anything happening in Orahovac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now I move to the time where you get this phone call from Trbic asking you to send some men, and my first question is: When, first of all, the men that you sent to Orahovac, they were taken from that intervention platoon that you had sent earlier to Tisova Kosa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: It was not an intervention platoon. It was a regular platoon made up of men from companies, because the intervention platoon was introduced in the schematic of the brigade. It was the Zolja platoon. This one was sort of improvised from, made up of men from various companies to perform that function.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I ask you this question, Mr. Ristic, just to clarify, because -- and I make reference here to page 39 of the transcript, lines 10 to 13, and also lines 14 to 17, just to confirm that those men that you sent to Orahovac, they were first taken away from the trenches to form that temporary platoon, and then they were taken, so they were already away from the trenches, and you took them to send them to Orahovac and that's why they were available. Is that correct? Can you answer, because I don't ...

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: It's common knowledge that they did that during the night, and during the day they were near the battalion command, available. They made ambushes only during the night. And that went on for only two nights. Later on the order came from the brigade command to pull them out from the Tisova Kosa area because there was a shortage of men. A large column of people was coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the man that -- one of your soldier called you to inform you or to ask you what was going on in Orahovac, and according to your testimony he said that they were ready to leave the trenches to go and defend their families in Orahovac. Now, would I be correct in saying that because you did not want them to leave the trenches because it was important to you that they would stay on the line, that that is why you sent those men to Orahovac at the request of Trbic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: When those people -- if those people left the line and went to Orahovac great problems would have been caused, and the situation would have been much worse, for the battalion included, because six trenches on the defence line mean a lot. The troops of the 2nd Corps were waiting for their opportunity when the line would be broken so that these people could go through, and if they had done that, they would have been putting the battalion at great risk. That's why I decided to send those men over there so that the men from the trenches wouldn't leave. I knew that the person I was talking to was volatile, and he was perfectly prepared to do what he was threatening to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'm not going to ask you any questions about what you saw in Orahovac. I'm going to move straight to the fact that when you returned to your command that night, and would I be right in saying that from that point on, now we're talking the 14th in the evening until the 15th, that your focus was on preparing your battalion because the column was coming your way? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that on the night of the 15th you were actually attacked at 4.30 in the a.m.? That was the first time you were attacked by the column; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: It's not the column that had attacked us. We were attacked by units of the 2nd Corps of the BH army at the point where our battalion linked with the 6th Battalion at around 4.30 of the morning of the 15th. I went straight there. I saw the attack with my own eyes and stayed there until it was all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I just have one question. I said I would not ask any questions about -- about Orahovac school, but I do have one question and that relates to Gojko Simic. Could you say -- would I be right in saying that Gojko Simic, he was at that time not on service from the 4th Battalion, because as you said you had been sent because his son was going -- was sent -- was being sent off for military duty. Now, I just ask you to confirm that this is the case, but that he was not the only one in that position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Nine men from the battalion were absent because they were seeing their sons off to the army. Their sons were recruits doing their military duty for the first time, and such leave is normally agreed with the command of the brigade, and they were absent. Around 10.00 or 11.00 in the morning of the 14th recruits gathered in front of the barracks at Karakaj, and then they are bussed to their various places where they are to serve their military service, and they are usually seen off by their family. So during those days Gojko Simic was busy doing that, and he was not present at the battalion those 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, two quick questions concerning this practice. Can you confirm that this was a regular practice to send the people on leave for the sake of attending their son's send-off to the army?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the practice, and nobody was ever denied leave for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in this case when those nine men, including Gojko Simic, were sent for that purpose, that was done with the knowledge of your commander who left on 1 July from the command of the 4th Battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move now to the 15th in the afternoon. You mentioned that Major Obrenovic arrived at your location, and I'd like you to confirm that this was sometime in the early afternoon of the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I take it that between the order you receive on the morning of the 14th of July and the time that Major Obrenovic arrives at the 4th Battalion command on the 15th in the afternoon, that you did not get any information from him during that period; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as you testified along with my colleague, during the time that he spent with you -- well, first let's start by the period that he was with you. That is from the 15th in the afternoon to the 16th in the afternoon when you withdraw from the battalion command. Is that the period that he was with you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: As you mentioned to my colleague, during this period you did not discuss with him the events that you had witnessed in Orahovac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't think so. I don't think we had time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I now move to a few questions I have concerning Major Obrenovic. Now, Major Obrenovic, of course, as you mention he was the man that was leading the operations or leading the combat activities in those days that is at least from the 12th until at least the 15th of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you are aware that Major Obrenovic was charged before this Tribunal in relation to the events which took place in Zvornik area after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you're also aware that he pleaded guilty and that he's now serving a prison sentence in relation to these events; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You mention in your testimony that you read his statement. Would I be correct that this is the statement of fact that you saw on the internet following his guilty plea?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be correct in saying that you were very surprised to read in that statement that he was involved in the Orahovac events, because he told you when he met with you that he knew nothing about it? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, that conversation when Major Obrenovic told you that he knew nothing about Orahovac, you answered that question from my colleague, but would I be correct that this happened somewhere in the year 2000 during the period before his arrest?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which year it was, but this was before he went to any questionings about the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that at that moment Major Obrenovic was preparing his defence and he asked you to come to his office to discuss these events; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: He called me and told me -- I heard from him that some of those who survived recognised Gojko Simic, and he asked me, too, where Gojko Simic was. So we talked a bit about Gojko Simic. I told him that Gojko Simic was absent because he was seeing his son to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in his statement of facts, the one that you read on the internet, and that is dated on the 20th of May, 2003, Obrenovic stated that he contacted you on 14 July and that you informed him on the radio, using coded language, that there were problems with the people who had been brought to Orahovac. My question is: Do you recall speaking to Obrenovic about the events in Orahovac on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that conversation. I think we didn't talk, because had we talked I probably would have remembered. We definitely didn't talk. As to how he stated that and why, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, I was quoting from page 3 of the statement of facts of -- provided by Dragan Obrenovic on the 20th of May, 2003. My next question, Mr. Ristic, is during your first interview at the public security station in Zvornik, now, this one took place on the 26th of August, 2003, and you -- there was a question posed to you by my colleague, you stated the following, and I quote -- that is on page 6 of this statement: "As regards Dragan Obrenovic claim that he talked to me on the radio using code about the events in Orahovac, I can say that this --" sorry "-- I can say that is not true. That is, we had no contact whatsoever." Do you stand by this statement which you provided to the security station in Zvornik on the 26th of August, 2003?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in his statement of facts, Obrenovic further stated, and I quote from pages 5 and 6, he stated first that he discussed with you -- now, I'm not quoting. He -- now, I quote from the statement, page 5 and 6. Obrenovic said: "I discussed military matters with Ristic and about an hour to an hour and a half later I reminded him about the conversation that we had on the 14th of July about the prisoners from Srebrenica." Am I right in saying that this conversation never took place? The one on the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember any conversation with Mr. Obrenovic about the events in Orahovac. I think that he gave a statement initially, maybe that is the case here, when he wanted to defend himself, on which occasion he said that he knew nothing with about it, and he said that he allegedly talked to me and that he heard from me. However, later on he admitted that he had known about the events, and this has nothing to do with me because I really don't remember anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will now read you, Mr. Ristic, portions of the judgement which was rendered by the Trial Chamber in the Blagojevic and Jokic case on 17 January 2005 and ask you some questions arising from what was mentioned in the judgement then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Bourgon. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I object to this line of questioning. I just -- I don't see what the relevance of it. If my learned friend wants to put a question to the witness with respect to a fact that might be contained in the judgement, that is a separate thing than reading the judgement to the witness and asking him to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There is a statement of facts the Trial Chamber took from the evidence it heard and draw conclusions about this witness who was not heard in that trial. So I want to ask him whether what is mentioned in the judgement he did or he did not do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes. I see you still standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am, Mr. President. The simple -- the simple matter is that if there is particular conduct of which the witness has been -- which has been attributed to the witness, then my learned friend can simply ask the question. It doesn't need to be predicated on the finding of a court or the judgement of a Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our decision, Mr. Bourgon, is please avoid to make specific reference to any of the judgements that you had in mind and put to the witness the facts that you would like him to give us information upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness, I will withdraw that question and move on to a next question. I come back to your first interview of the public security station in Zvornik on 26 August 2003, where you stated the following -- I quote from page 6 of your statement where you said: "When he came to the battalion on the 15th of July, that is Major Obrenovic, we did not talk about Orahovac, that is about the prisoners from Srebrenica." Do you stick by this statement today?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I refer now to the statement of facts provided by Obrenovic, on page 6. Obrenovic stated the following: During this alleged conversation on the 15th of July at the command of the 4th Battalion, Obrenovic said you told him that when you lined up your men at the school in Orahovac Drago Nikolic requested your men to stay and if they did they would all be issued with new uniforms by Milosevic. Did you ever say this to Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: No. I did not see Drago Nikolic when I came there, and I could not have stated what he said I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: During your first interview at the public security station in Zvornik, the one on 26 August 2003, you stated the following: "It is not true that I was stopped by Drago Nikolic when I was lining up my men in order to take them away since Drago Nikolic was not there at all while I lined up the men." Do you stick with this statement today?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in the statement of facts provided by Obrenovic, Obrenovic stated, and I quote -- this is from page 6 of the statement of facts by Obrenovic: "I learned later from Ristic that a certain Gojko Simic from the 4th Battalion had been on leave at that time, but because he was from Orahovac he went there voluntarily and joined the guards at the gymnasium before the arrival of the 4th Battalion reinforcements. Ristic said that Drago Nikolic had been asking for volunteers, and Gojko had volunteered to take part in the execution of prisoners." Did you ever mention this to Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I didn't. I don't know how it was. All I know is that Gojko Simic was absent. Now, as to he joined the guards, how he joined them, I don't know about that because I didn't see it. I think that Mr. Obrenovic, as he was making the preparations, talked to a lot of people about the events, and then he put the picture together in a way. I could not have talked about Drago since he wasn't there. I could not have talked about the participation of Gojko Simic because I didn't see that. I'm only talking about things that I saw. Now, assumptions, yes, everybody can make assumptions this way or that way, and it was probably his judgement to volunteer this. If he came there, he may have been irritated because his rival had been snatched with him and he was the company commander. Now, as to where he was and what he saw, I don't know. I didn't look into this. If this man were alive today then one could ask him, but since he got killed, I never inquired about these details afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you never -- that is speculation, and you never mentioned that to Obrenovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Correct. There was some talk about Gojko Simic, but I didn't put it in those terms. Perhaps he heard this from somebody else. I didn't tell him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And am I correct in saying that you never told Major Obrenovic that Drago Nikolic had been asking for volunteers for the executions?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that. How would I know that when I didn't participate in it and I wasn't there? Who did it and how they did it is something that I can't talk about because I didn't see it. What I saw is what I told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to come back on the fact that Obrenovic did call you to come and see him in his office, and he also called you on the phone to discuss these events; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that on that moment he told you that he knew nothing about the events in Orahovac and you believed him.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: He told me before. I think so. It's difficult for me to know all the details now. But when I came to talk to him about Gojko Simic, I was still convinced and I thought that he knew nothing about it because that's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in the -- regarding the -- Dragan Obrenovic, he testified in the trial of Blagojevic and Jokic, and when he testified before that Trial Chamber under oath, he said the following: "I learned from Lazar Ristic, that Gojko Simic a member of the 4th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade had joined the first group of who were guarding the school and had later volunteered to participate in the killings." My understanding is that you never said this to Dragan Obrenovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I didn't say this. I didn't know what Gojko Simic did. I don't know who was the source of information. I don't know anything about this. All I know is what I saw when I came and during the brief period of time that I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when he testified before the Trial Chamber under oath, Dragan Obrenovic said that he was told by you, Lazar Ristic, that Drago Nikolic participated in the killings in Orahovac. Did you ever see this to Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did anyone ever inform you or did you obtain any information from any source that Drago Nikolic participated in the killings in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I did not hear any stories nor did I look into what Drago Nikolic did, or other individuals. I'm stating only facts here, what I saw and events in which I participated. As for the stories about who was where, I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My last question concerning Dragan Obrenovic is the following: We have information which was provided to us by the Prosecution concerning an individual called Milan Maric, who said that before Dragan Obrenovic was arrested and transferred to The Hague he was actively preparing his defence, and he contacted a number of persons, members of the Zvornik Brigade, including, amongst other, Ostoja Stanisic and you. Can you confirm this information?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I talked to him and the conversation concerned only Gojko Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question refers to your knowledge, your personal knowledge of Drago Nikolic. In response to a question which was asked of you by the Prosecution, you stated that you were the assistant commander for security of the 4th Battalion for a period of approximately two years. So I take it that you had the opportunity to work with Drago Nikolic, who was the chief of security. What can you say about the qualities and the competencies of Drago Nikolic as an officer and as the chief of security of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I met Drago Nikolic for the first time in March of 1993. At that time, at the proposal of the commander of the 4th Battalion, I was nominated to the post of assistant commander for security, as a result of which I went to the headquarters, at which time I had a brief meeting with Drago Nikolic who was chief of security within the Zvornik Brigade. The conversation centred around the fact that I was not familiar with security issues, that I never attended even any training or anything of the sort about the work conducted by officers, and I told him that he would need to instruct me and that I would follow his instructions. Later on when we worked together and when we had meetings, his assistance to me strictly concerned the work of security organs in the battalions. His instructions were very specific, and I never had any problems with him. I think that my attitude, my decent attitude towards work and the post that I held was such that I abided by the rules and I was among the best in the battalion. Many people in the brigade and in the battalion were aware of this. Now, about his instructions and advice to me, what he told me was that we needed to monitor enemy positions, that we needed to have contact with our people on defence lines, that we had to tour our lines, that we had to identify individuals who deserted the positions and had destructive behaviour. So this is what we dealt with with the people who abandoned positions and deserted, and we wanted to deal with them so that others wouldn't suffer. And that's the kind of advice that he gave me. It was about the security issues in the battalion and the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, it's my understanding, Mr. Ristic, that you now know what happened in Orahovac about the killings of prisoners. My question is: Could you tell the Trial Chamber whether in your opinion Drago Nikolic is the kind of person who could be involved and/or organise such atrocious killings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I object on the grounds of relevance, and secondly, I don't think that my learned friend has laid a sufficient foundation for the question to be based. He hasn't established the nature and the extent of the relationship between the witness and the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the witness needs to remove his headphones for a short while. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is straightforward character evidence question. I'm trying to get character evidence from the witness. He's worked with him for two years. He knows him. He can say what he believes and the Trial Chamber can draw the conclusion from his answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We are going to allow the question, Mr. Bourgon, with the understanding that I'm sure you appreciate that out of every hundred persons that commit homicide, murder, if you were to put the question would you have expected this person to commit -- there would be very, very few who would be classified as persons who are prone to commit murder. "Yes, I would have expected him to commit murder." So do consider the probative value attached to your question, and you're free to rephrase it if you wish to. One moment, because we have to tell the witness to put on his headphone again. It's up to you. I mean ... Do you want me to repeat --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Ristic, can you assist the Trial Chamber regarding Drago Nikolic and tell us according to what you saw from him what his attitude was towards Muslims?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: You mean during the entire war?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: I did not have occasion to talk to him about that issue. Simply, our conversations were of a military nature. I never talked to him about Muslims or some other issues, so I can't really give you a specific answer about his attitude. I never heard from him or from anybody down there at the headquarters that there was any hate, that they talked about any hate, hatred. We simply spoke about military issues, military regulations, and that's what we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I just have one more question and then I will have some -- something to say to the Trial Chamber, but do you -- would I be right in saying that -- I come back now because I forgot one question. On the night of the 13th of July when you were in your battalion command, it is my understanding that you received a phone call from Drago Nikolic who was then at the IKM. Can you confirm and explain what this conversation was about?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR RISTIC
utterances.text: On the 13th I noticed in the battalion headquarters, in the sector of Srpski Nezuk where the houses were destroyed, and above those houses there was a hill on which I noticed a large white flag. I saw it, but I didn't know what it was. Towards the evening, as it was getting dark Drago Nikolic called me from the IKM, from the forward command post. I didn't know who was on duty that night. He called me from the IKM and asked me whether I saw fire by the mosque in the Muslim Nezuk. I told him -- or, rather, I went out to see this fire, and our conversation centred around the fact that, yes, I did see it, but I didn't know what it was it. It was only later that I found out that this had to do with the columns moving towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We have to stop with the witness's testimony here today. Witness, we will continue tomorrow. Between now and until you finish your testimony, you are not to contact anyone or allow anyone to contact you to discuss the subject matter of your testimony. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon. He can be escorted. Very briefly because --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have to miss the beginning of tomorrow's session, and I asked my colleagues of the Prosecution whether I could interrupt my cross-examination and resume him. Maybe it will not be necessary depending on what the others ask, but the Prosecution has agreed. So my colleague would do his cross-examination. I would come back after for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem. All right. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 17th day of April, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.
